blk_part_01_funny_food_names_in_cologne.text: Almost every menu in a Cologne brewery pub has a dish called Halve Hahn. In the dialect of Cologne, the local way of speaking, the name says half a rooster. A rooster is a male chicken. But when your plate arrives, there is no chicken on it.

blk_part_01_funny_food_names_in_cologne.text: A Halve Hahn is half of a Röggelchen, a small, dark rye roll. You met this roll in the beer lesson. Bakers put the rolls in the oven in pairs, so two rolls touch and bake together. Later they break them apart. On your half you get butter, a thick slice of Gouda, strong mustard and rings of raw onion. Gouda is a yellow cheese from the Netherlands. It is soft and a little salty.

blk_part_01_funny_food_names_in_cologne.text: So why the funny name? Nobody knows for sure, and people in Cologne tell different stories. The best-known story takes place at a birthday party in the late 1800s. As a joke, a man ordered half a rooster for each of his friends. He told the waiter his plan first. The friends waited for roast chicken, but the waiter brought rye rolls with cheese. Everyone laughed, and the joke became the name of the dish. It is a nice story, but nobody can say if it is true.

The brand ABB says its story starts with that factory. Since 2012, Düsseldorfer Mostert has been a protected name in the European Union. Only mustard made in Düsseldorf may use this name. A company in another city can make mustard in the same way. But it cannot call it Düsseldorfer Mostert. Kölsch has a protected name too. In both cases, the name tells you where the product really comes from.

blk_part_04_a_pepper_stew_in_dortmund.text: Pfefferpotthast is a beef stew: meat cooked slowly in liquid until it is very soft. It is an old dish of Westphalia, the region around Dortmund. It was a meal for working people. The cook fries pieces of beef. Then the beef boils slowly in a pot for a long time, with lots of onions. Bay leaves and plenty of black pepper go in too. The onions almost melt and make the stew sweet, and the pepper makes it spicy.

blk_part_05_christmas_markets_in_decembe.text: The favourite market food in Cologne is Reibekuchen: fried potato pancakes. The cook grates raw potatoes and onions into tiny pieces. Then the cook presses out the water and adds egg, flour and salt. Spoons of this mix go into hot oil. They fry until they are brown, crispy at the edges and soft in the middle. You eat them hot, with apple sauce. In the Rhineland, people also eat them with Rübenkraut, the sugar-beet syrup from the Sauerbraten part. Hot, salty potato with something sweet is a popular mix here.
